items.title: The Court That Never Was
items.one_line: A man the bar council once jailed for practising law without a degree rents an office, calls it a tribunal, and spends five years settling other people's land disputes — until the litigants who won discover their victories were never real.
items.mechanism: He did not forge a single document that mattered. He rented an office, furnished it to look like a courtroom, hired staff to play court personnel, and told people he was an arbitrator appointed by a competent court. Nobody asked to see the appointment. Litigants tired of waiting years for a real hearing paid him a fee for a fast one, and he gave them a ruling on paper that looked exactly like a ruling. The illusion held because the thing he was impersonating is one almost nobody has ever seen up close.
items.engine: Every judgment he delivers has to be protected by the next one. The moment any losing party takes his order to a real court and finds no record of the case, five years of rulings unwind at once — so he cannot refuse a new client, cannot rule against anyone powerful enough to check, and cannot stop. The con is not a scheme with an end; it is a standing obligation that grows every week he keeps it.

cast.motive: to be addressed the way he was refused the right to be addressed

cast.name_or_role: his clerk, hired to play court staff
cast.motive: a salary, and the first respectable job of her life

cast.name_or_role: a woman who won her father's land in his court
cast.motive: to keep what she believes a judge awarded her

cast.name_or_role: the brother she beat, who accepted the ruling
cast.motive: to be the kind of man who obeys a court

cast.name_or_role: the real advocate who noticed the seal was wrong
cast.motive: professional disgust, and an old grudge

cast.name_or_role: the bar council officer who struck him off in 2007
cast.motive: to be proved right a second time

reasons: A living private individual, arrested and charged, not convicted — every claim about him is an allegation until a court says otherwise.
The litigants are private people who were defrauded. They are victims and cannot be identifiable.
Change the state, the names, the profession he came from, and the year. The mechanism is what we are adapting, not the man.

facts.what_happened: A man ran a fake court out of an office in Gandhinagar, Gujarat, passing judgments for about five years from 2019 until his arrest in October 2024.
He told clients he was an arbitrator appointed by a competent court to settle their disputes.
He furnished the office to resemble a courtroom and used staff acting as court personnel to complete the illusion.
He targeted people in land disputes by offering a fast ruling for a heavy fee, against real courts' long delays.
His rulings touched more than 100 acres across at least 11 properties, and 10 of those cases were still unresolved when the court was exposed.
He was jailed for three months in 2007 after the state bar council said he held no valid law degree and was practising as a lawyer.
He was arrested under IPC 170, pretending to hold office as a public servant, and IPC 419, cheating by personation.

items.why_this_sells: It is a dominance fantasy built on a humiliation that actually happened: a man told by an institution that he was not real, who then simply declared himself real and was believed for five years. The listener gets the fantasy of the nobody who stops asking permission, and the dread of watching him need one more lie every episode to hold up the last one. And the side characters are the product — every litigant who won in that room walked out happy and does not know it was nothing, which is a whole serial per person, none of which can contradict the mainline because none of them were ever told.
items.why_not: The protagonist is a fraud with real victims, and a season that enjoys his cleverness too much becomes a story that thinks defrauding poor litigants is charming. He also has no legal jeopardy for most of the run — nobody is chasing him — so the pressure has to come from inside the con rather than from a pursuer, which is harder to write and easy to get wrong.
items.text: A man the bar council once jailed for practising law without a degree rents an office, calls it a tribunal, and spends five years settling other people's land disputes — until the litigants who won discover their victories were never real.

items.title: The Mandsaur Woman Who Was Already Cremated
items.one_line: After her family cremates a crushed body and four men sit in jail for her murder, a missing mother walks into the police station alive—then has to prove she is herself while nobody can say whose body was burned.
items.where: Mandsaur and Jhabua districts, Madhya Pradesh, India
items.mechanism: A missing woman’s family identified a badly damaged body using a tattoo and black thread, performed her last rites, and triggered a murder case; 18 months later she returned, claiming she had been taken away and sold to another man.
items.engine: The woman is alive but officially entangled with a dead body, four jailed suspects, a disputed trafficking account, and an unidentified victim whose real identity must be uncovered.

cast.motive: To establish that she is alive, recover her children, and control the story of where she spent 18 months.

cast.name_or_role: The father who identified the body
cast.motive: To defend an identification that destroyed another family and may have helped imprison four men.
To escape a murder case built around a corpse that may not be the missing woman.

cast.name_or_role: The two men named in the alleged sale
cast.motive: To deny, conceal, or profit from the woman’s account of being moved to Kota.

cast.name_or_role: The police officer reopening the case
cast.motive: To determine whether the returned woman is genuine and repair a failed investigation.

cast.name_or_role: The children waiting for their mother
cast.motive: To accept a woman everyone had taught them was dead.

reasons: The real participants are living private individuals and the case remains recent.
The alleged sale and confinement account must not be presented as established fact without court verification.
Change names, village and districts, the children’s details, and the precise identity of the alleged traffickers.
Tell the serial through fictionalised investigators, family members and the unidentified dead woman’s relatives rather than exposing the real family.

facts.what_happened: NDTV reported that a 35-year-old woman returned to her village after being presumed murdered and cremated, while four men remained in jail in connection with the supposed murder.
The woman’s father said the family identified the damaged body using a tattoo and a black thread around the leg, then performed the last rites.
Police said the woman claimed she had gone with a man named Shahrukh, who allegedly sold her to another man for Rs 5 lakh; she said she lived in Kota for 18 months before escaping.
The four accused—Imran, Shahrukh, Sonu and Ejaz—were reported to be in jail pending trial and had petitioned the local court after the woman’s reappearance.

The Jhabua superintendent of police said police would conduct medical examination and DNA testing and record witness statements before conclusively establishing that the returned woman was the same person believed to have been murdered.

India Today reported that the woman supplied Aadhaar and voter ID documents and that neighbours and family members confirmed her identity, while the police had registered the original murder case after the family identified the mutilated body.

items.why_this_sells: The instant fear is brutally recognisable: your family performs your funeral, strangers are punished for your death, and returning home does not prove who you are.
items.why_not: The central trafficking account is still only an allegation, so the series needs heavy fictionalisation and must preserve uncertainty rather than claim a solved truth.
items.text: After her family cremates a crushed body and four men sit in jail for her murder, a missing mother walks into the police station alive—then has to prove she is herself while nobody can say whose body was burned. A missing woman’s family identified a badly damaged body using a tattoo and black thread, performed her last rites, and triggered a murder case; 18 months later she returned, claiming she had been taken away and sold to another man.

items.title: The Beggar Who Collected Interest
items.one_line: In Indore, a man everyone treated as helpless street poor kept the beggar persona alive while quietly owning homes, rental vehicles and a private lending book.
items.where: Sarafa Bazaar, Indore, Madhya Pradesh, India
items.mechanism: A disabled-looking street beggar travelled on a wheeled board, accepted small donations without openly demanding them, collected interest payments from borrowers and controlled income-producing assets that the public did not know he owned.
items.engine: Every day he must preserve the image of helplessness in public while managing borrowers, tenants, vehicles, officials, family pressure and the risk that one visible luxury will expose the entire hidden life.

cast.motive: He needs the street persona for cash flow, anonymity and psychological control over the people who pity him.
They need quick money but become vulnerable when the supposedly powerless lender demands repayment.
They depend on his autos and car while knowing more about his real wealth than his donors do.
They want a beggar-free city and must decide whether he is a victim, a fraud or an unexpectedly successful informal businessman.
He wants to rehabilitate the man but discovers that removing him from the street may destroy his lending network.

cast.name_or_role: The abandoned family and village contacts
cast.motive: They carry the buried history of illness, rejection and the question of who helped him build the hidden property base.

reasons: The principal is a living private individual identified by name in recent reporting.
Change the name, town, market, illness, property count and vehicle details.
Use a fictional composite of the rescue officials, borrowers and family rather than reproducing identifiable real people.
Avoid stating that any individual committed fraud; frame the hidden-income mechanism as reported and fictionalize the legal and administrative consequences.

facts.what_happened: AajTak reported that a man known in Indore's Sarafa area as a disabled beggar moved around on a wheeled board and received money from passers-by.
The report said officials discovered that he owned three permanent houses, three autorickshaws and a Maruti Dzire car.
NDTV reported that one house had been provided through government assistance while two were said to have been purchased by him.
According to the man's account reported by NDTV, the three autos and the car operated as taxis and generated income while he continued appearing in the market as a beggar.
NDTV reported his claim that about four lakh rupees had been lent at interest and produced roughly two thousand rupees a day.
The authorities sent him to a shelter, while he reportedly warned that being kept away from the market could cause his outstanding lending money to disappear.

items.why_this_sells: The instantly recognisable fear is that the person everyone pities has been studying them, earning from them and hiding a second life in plain sight.
items.why_not: The raw event is recent and lightly documented, so the long-running borrower and family conflicts must be fictionalised rather than presented as established fact.
items.text: In Indore, a man everyone treated as helpless street poor kept the beggar persona alive while quietly owning homes, rental vehicles and a private lending book. A disabled-looking street beggar travelled on a wheeled board, accepted small donations without openly demanding them, collected interest payments from borrowers and controlled income-producing assets that the public did not know he owned.

items.title: The Man Who Died Twice
items.one_line: After his wife’s family gets him booked for harassment, a furious husband disappears, lets them build a murder case around his ‘death’, then watches from another city as the people he blames are dragged into court.
items.where: Maharajganj, Uttar Pradesh / Mira Road, Maharashtra, India
items.mechanism: Pannelal Yadav allegedly staged his own murder, disappeared under another identity, and allowed his family to accuse his wife and in-laws of killing him and destroying the evidence.
items.engine: The revenge stays alive as long as the ‘dead’ man maintains his false identity while his family, police, lawyers and in-laws fight over a murder that never happened.

cast.name_or_role: Pannelal Yadav, the supposedly murdered husband
cast.motive: To punish his wife and in-laws after a harassment case and settlement left him resentful.
To survive the original marital dispute and avoid being blamed for a murder she says never happened.
To defend themselves after being accused of killing and disposing of Pannelal.
To help sustain the death story and push police and court authorities to register a murder case.
To identify a man hiding under another identity and unravel the apparently impossible murder.

cast.name_or_role: The local police and court system
cast.motive: To determine whether the missing man was murdered or whether the entire case was manufactured.

reasons: The reported incident involves living private individuals and allegations attributed to police reporting.
Change names, villages, police jurisdictions and family details; make the protagonist and all relatives fictional composites.
Tell the story primarily through the wife, investigator and supposedly dead man rather than asserting guilt as established fact.

prior_adaptations: No specific film or series adaptation of this reported Uttar Pradesh/Maharashtra incident was found in the searches.
Generic fake-death and revenge dramas are near-misses, not adaptations of this particular event.

facts.what_happened: Hindustan Times reported that Pannelal Yadav was arrested after allegedly staging his own murder to implicate his wife and in-laws.
The report said Yadav and his family had previously faced a criminal case after his wife alleged harassment, and that the sides later settled the matter.
According to the report, Yadav disappeared after visiting his in-laws in Maharajganj, Uttar Pradesh, on October 15, 2016.

His family allegedly suspected that his wife and her relatives had murdered him and disposed of his body; when local police refused the complaint, the family approached court and a murder case was registered.
Mumbai Crime Branch reportedly found Yadav hiding in Mira Road for about two years under a different identity and identified him as the man reported murdered in Uttar Pradesh.
A deputy commissioner of police was quoted as saying that the investigation also revealed family involvement.

items.why_this_sells: The instantly recognisable fear is being declared a murderer by your own family while the dead person is secretly alive and watching the case grow.
items.why_not: The real-world incident appears to have been exposed within roughly two years, so the 150-episode engine requires fictionalised complications inside the false-murder case rather than literal biography.
items.text: After his wife’s family gets him booked for harassment, a furious husband disappears, lets them build a murder case around his ‘death’, then watches from another city as the people he blames are dragged into court. Pannelal Yadav allegedly staged his own murder, disappeared under another identity, and allowed his family to accuse his wife and in-laws of killing him and destroying the evidence.

items.title: The Irrigation Office That Never Existed
items.one_line: In a tribal Gujarat town, a fake executive engineer builds a working government department—with staff, seals, sanctioned-looking files and insiders—until twelve “pending projects” force the real administration to ask where its own office is.
items.where: Bodeli, Chhota Udepur district, Gujarat, India
items.mechanism: A rented office was presented as the government’s Irrigation Project Division. The principal operator allegedly posed as an executive engineer, while an accomplice supplied the office, documents and workflow; current and retired government employees allegedly prepared, typed, signed and routed proposals using forged seals and signatures.
items.engine: Every new project, signature, inspection, payment and departmental query requires the fake office to recruit another insider, create another document and make the invented department look more real.

cast.name_or_role: Sandeep Rajput, alleged fake executive engineer
cast.motive: Money, authority and the thrill of making a nonexistent department obeyed like a real one.

cast.name_or_role: Abu-Bakr Saiyyad, contractor and alleged office operator
cast.motive: Access to government-funded work and control of the physical machinery behind the deception.

cast.name_or_role: Javid Ibrahim Maknojiya, junior clerk and FIR complainant later arrested
cast.motive: Possible participation followed by an attempt to redirect blame when the scheme surfaced.

cast.name_or_role: Chandu Purshottam Kareliya, retired tribal-development officer
cast.motive: Allegedly lending former official credibility and signatures to keep the paperwork alive.
Turning raw proposals into convincing government files without asking who legally owned the office.
Some seek legitimate project approvals, some allegedly protect the arrangement, and others fear being blamed for missing public money.

cast.name_or_role: Villagers and contractors awaiting irrigation projects
cast.motive: They need roads, water and work, making them vulnerable to promises bearing an official seal.

cast.name_or_role: Project Administrator Sunil Kumar and the SIT
cast.motive: Find out how a phantom office generated a pipeline of official-looking projects inside the real bureaucracy.

reasons: The case is recent and the named principals and officials may be living.
Change names, town, district and departmental designation; fictionalize the exact project list and make the central viewpoint a composite clerk or contractor.
Retain the mechanism of a fake public office, but avoid asserting guilt beyond what a court establishes.

facts.what_happened: Police investigated a fake government office operating under the name “Irrigation Project Division” in Bodeli taluka, Chhota Udepur.
Police said Sandeep Rajput posed as an executive engineer and worked with contractor Abu-Bakr Saiyyad.
The investigation reportedly involved five arrests, including a junior clerk and a retired assistant tribal-development officer who were connected to the department named in the FIR.

Officials questioned why twelve pending projects had been sent for approval to the department; investigators said proposals were prepared by the junior clerk, typed at the contractor’s office and then signed by the retired officer.
Police raided an office in a shopping complex and found government-scheme details displayed on the walls, seizing documents and other materials.
The accused were booked under provisions covering impersonating a public servant, cheating by personation, forgery, use of forged documents, counterfeit seals and criminal conspiracy.
Investigators were also examining whether the alleged operator had used the same method in Dahod district.

items.why_this_sells: The instantly recognisable fear is that an official stamp, office room and confident voice can make an invented authority more powerful than the real one.
items.why_not: The public record currently describes an investigation rather than a final adjudication, so the drama must fictionalize aggressively and treat several roles as allegations.
items.text: In a tribal Gujarat town, a fake executive engineer builds a working government department—with staff, seals, sanctioned-looking files and insiders—until twelve “pending projects” force the real administration to ask where its own office is. A rented office was presented as the government’s Irrigation Project Division. The principal operator allegedly posed as an executive engineer, while an accomplice supplied the office, documents and workflow; current and retired government employees allegedly prepared, typed, signed and routed proposals using forged seals and signatures.

items.title: The Son Who Erased the Heirs
items.one_line: After his railway-worker father dies, a son quietly changes the death date, manufactures a sole-heir certificate, and sells the family plot before his mother and five siblings even know they have been disinherited.
items.where: Thaneerkulam village, Tiruvallur district, Tamil Nadu, India
items.mechanism: The accused allegedly used a forged death certificate showing his father died in 2019—years after the reported 1999 death—and a false legal-heir certificate naming himself as the only successor, allowing him to sell the plot without the other heirs' knowledge.
items.engine: The family must keep proving that the father died when everyone says he did, while every revenue record, sale document, official witness and family alliance becomes another battlefield over who legally exists as an heir.

cast.name_or_role: The fifth son accused of the fraud
cast.motive: He wants the entire plot and the money from its sale, and must keep the forged official story intact.
She must recover the property while confronting the son she trusted and protecting the family's records.
Each sibling has a different need for the inheritance and a different opinion about whether to expose their brother.
His real death date, employment history and property purchase become the hidden timeline that can destroy the fraud.
They must reconstruct how death and heirship records passed through official channels.
The buyer wants a clean title and may turn against the family once the sale is challenged.
They may have accepted money, been deceived, or need to protect themselves from prosecution.

reasons: The case is recent and the accused, mother, siblings, purchaser and officials may be living private individuals.
Change all names, the village, the property value and the family composition; use a fictional district and composite officials.
Tell the story through the excluded mother's and siblings' fight to restore the record, rather than presenting unproved allegations as established guilt.
Retain the mechanism but fictionalise the exact documents, dates and investigative outcome unless independently verified in court records.

facts.what_happened: The New Indian Express reported that Avadi City Police arrested a 41-year-old man accused of selling his deceased father's property using forged death and heirship certificates, excluding his mother and five siblings.
The report identified the accused as Alphonse Raj, the fifth son of P Susila and the late Ponnusamy.
Police said Ponnusamy had purchased a 2,100-square-foot vacant plot in Thaneerkulam village, Tiruvallur district, in 1988.
The article said Ponnusamy died in 1999, while the allegedly forged death certificate claimed that he died in April 2019, when the mother was still alive.
Police said a false legal-heir certificate named the accused as the sole successor, after which he sold the property, valued at about Rs 34 lakh, without the family's knowledge.
The Land Fraud Investigation Wing of the Avadi Central Crime Branch registered a case under Sections 420, 468, 467 and 465 of the IPC, according to the report.
The report said a special police team apprehended the accused and he was remanded in judicial custody.

items.why_this_sells: The instantly recognisable fear is that a trusted son can make a family disappear from its own inheritance using one official-looking piece of paper.
items.why_not: The public record currently gives the arrest and mechanism but little documented aftermath, so the long legal and emotional middle would need careful fictional expansion.
items.text: After his railway-worker father dies, a son quietly changes the death date, manufactures a sole-heir certificate, and sells the family plot before his mother and five siblings even know they have been disinherited. The accused allegedly used a forged death certificate showing his father died in 2019—years after the reported 1999 death—and a false legal-heir certificate naming himself as the only successor, allowing him to sell the plot without the other heirs' knowledge.

items.title: The Twenty Cheques for One House
items.one_line: A desperate Delhi borrower gives a neighbourhood lender twenty blank cheques and his house papers for a loan, then discovers the bargain may have turned him from owner into tenant.
items.mechanism: A ₹1.5 lakh loan was allegedly secured with twenty blank cheques and the original possession slip of the borrower’s home; after repayment disputes, the lender asserted that the house had actually been sold and leased back to the borrower.
items.engine: The debt never ends when the security itself becomes the battlefield: each cheque, instalment, notice, family witness and possession threat can reopen whether the borrower is a debtor, tenant or owner.

cast.motive: Needs urgent money but must keep his family inside the only home they have.
Wants either repayment, control of the property or both, while preserving a respectable local-business identity.
Tries to renegotiate instalments and becomes the family’s financial fixer and witness.
Protects the household from eviction while questioning what her husband signed.
Recover the possession papers and preserve the family home after the borrower’s death.
Their signatures and recollections decide whether the paperwork was a loan, sale or lease.
Must decide whether the dispute is fraud, debt recovery, property possession or a private civil fight.

reasons: The underlying case is recent and the named parties may be living or represented by living heirs.
Change names, locality, property number and exact loan figures.
Tell the story through fictional borrowers, adult heirs and composite officials rather than reproducing allegations about identifiable private citizens.

facts.what_happened: The judgment records the borrower’s account that he sought a ₹1,50,000 loan in May 2003 and was asked to provide twenty blank cheques and the original possession slip of his property as security.
The borrower’s account says repayment was arranged through monthly instalments of ₹6,000, later reduced to ₹4,500, with additional payments made by his brother.
The borrower alleged that, after repayment disputes, the lender sent a notice claiming ownership of the house, declared the borrower a tenant and demanded rent and possession.
The lender’s defence was that the property had been voluntarily sold for ₹3 lakh, followed by a lease allowing the borrower to remain in the premises as a tenant.
The case involved competing claims over registered sale documents, a general power of attorney, a will, a lease deed, possession papers and multiple cheques.
The court found the lender’s claim of rent was doubtful, noting that the evidence did not make the alleged tenancy commercially convincing.
The judgment ultimately treated the transaction as securing a loan rather than a genuine sale, while requiring restoration of the money received before cancellation of the instruments.

items.why_this_sells: The instant fear is recognisable: one signature made during a money emergency can turn the family home, every cheque and every knock at the door into a new payment deadline.
items.why_not: The court record contains sharply conflicting versions, so the adaptation must fictionalize aggressively and preserve uncertainty rather than present every allegation as fact.
items.text: A desperate Delhi borrower gives a neighbourhood lender twenty blank cheques and his house papers for a loan, then discovers the bargain may have turned him from owner into tenant. A ₹1.5 lakh loan was allegedly secured with twenty blank cheques and the original possession slip of the borrower’s home; after repayment disputes, the lender asserted that the house had actually been sold and leased back to the borrower.

items.title: The Motihari Haunted-House Tenant
items.one_line: A family desperate to escape the spirits said killed their sons lets a holy man move into one room—then he turns the exorcism into a decades-long battle over rent, possession and ownership.
items.mechanism: A self-proclaimed spiritual healer occupies part of a supposedly haunted house to drive out evil spirits, then denies being a tenant and supports a rival purchaser’s claim to the property.
items.engine: The house remains contested between the family, the healer and a purchaser, while every ritual, rent demand and legal filing can reveal whether the haunting was genuine, exploited or staged.

cast.motive: Reclaim the family house and remove the occupant who entered under the pretext of spiritual protection.
Protect the home while trying to solve a family tragedy and later control its sale.

cast.name_or_role: Mohammed Manzurool Haque, the spiritual healer
cast.motive: Maintain his claim that he was invited as a supernatural protector, not rented as a tenant.
Secure possession after an agreement to buy the house and use the healer’s claim to strengthen his case.

cast.name_or_role: The two dead sons, as remembered by the household
cast.motive: Their deaths are the emotional source of the haunting claim and the mystery beneath the property dispute.
Separate tenancy, possession and sale claims from supernatural testimony.

reasons: The litigation names real parties and concerns a real private residence.
Change names, Motihari, the family history and the precise property details.
Tell the story primarily through a fictional tenant, a grieving household and a court clerk rather than presenting supernatural claims as verified fact.

facts.what_happened: The Supreme Court record says the owners sought eviction of a man occupying part of their residential house and alleged that he had been allowed in because he claimed spiritual powers.

In his written statement, the occupant said the owners believed evil spirits had killed their two sons and had asked him to use spiritual power to drive them away; he said he entered one room in 1978.
The occupant denied a landlord-tenant relationship and instead claimed that the family had benefited from his blessings and spiritual presence.
The record says a separate purchaser claimed that an agreement for sale had been executed on January 9, 1982, and that possession had been delivered to him.
The title suit and eviction suit were clubbed because they concerned the same house, creating a three-way dispute over tenancy, sale and possession.
The Supreme Court stated that mere execution of an agreement for sale did not itself confer title or legal possession and allowed the eviction-related claim to proceed against the occupant.

items.why_this_sells: The instantly recognisable fear is that a family invites a spiritual protector into a haunted home and discovers it may never be able to make him leave.
items.why_not: The supernatural evidence is entirely contested, so the adaptation must sustain ambiguity without inventing paranormal proof.
items.text: A family desperate to escape the spirits said killed their sons lets a holy man move into one room—then he turns the exorcism into a decades-long battle over rent, possession and ownership. A self-proclaimed spiritual healer occupies part of a supposedly haunted house to drive out evil spirits, then denies being a tenant and supports a rival purchaser’s claim to the property.

items.title: The Bride Who Was Abducted After Every Wedding
items.one_line: A young woman becomes Kajal, Seema, Neha and Sweety across four states, marries desperate families, then vanishes in a staged kidnapping—only to create the next identity and wedding. ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/lucknow/unhappily-ever-after-daku-dulhanwho-duped-12-grooms-arrested-in-up/amp_articleshow/120803107.cms))
items.where: Ambedkar Nagar and Jaunpur, Uttar Pradesh; operations spanning Gujarat, Haryana, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, India
items.mechanism: Gulshana allegedly used different names and fake identity documents, entered matrimonial negotiations through multiple channels, collected a settlement amount, staged a post-wedding abduction with gang members posing as relatives or attackers, and returned to matrimonial platforms under a new identity. ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/lucknow/unhappily-ever-after-daku-dulhanwho-duped-12-grooms-arrested-in-up/amp_articleshow/120803107.cms))
items.engine: Every new match creates another household to infiltrate, another alias to protect, another fake relative to recruit, and another groom whose family can expose the previous life.

cast.motive: Money, survival and control of the gang’s repeatable marriage con

cast.name_or_role: The husband who takes a five-percent cut
cast.motive: Profit and loyalty to the operation while maintaining a respectable married life
Cash, access to valuables and the thrill of performing the same disappearance in new towns
Commission for finding families desperate enough to overlook verification

cast.name_or_role: The latest groom and his family
cast.motive: A marriage bargain that turns into humiliation, financial loss and a hunt for the missing bride

cast.name_or_role: The police team that breaks the pattern
cast.motive: Recovering the latest victim’s property while discovering the syndicate’s older aliases

reasons: The principals are living and the reporting describes allegations and an arrest rather than final convictions.
Change names, towns, aliases, matrimonial platforms and physical details; use a composite groom and fictional gang.
Tell the story from the families and investigators’ point of view rather than exposing identifiable private individuals as established criminals.

facts.what_happened: The Times of India reported that Ambedkar Nagar police arrested Gulshana and eight alleged gang members after a wedding-scam operation involving at least twelve families. ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/lucknow/unhappily-ever-after-daku-dulhanwho-duped-12-grooms-arrested-in-up/amp_articleshow/120803107.cms))

The report said the woman used the names Kajal in Gujarat, Seema in Haryana, Neha in Bihar and Sweety in Uttar Pradesh. ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/lucknow/unhappily-ever-after-daku-dulhanwho-duped-12-grooms-arrested-in-up/amp_articleshow/120803107.cms))

Police said the gang negotiated money from families seeking matches, arranged the wedding, then staged an abduction in which male gang members escaped with jewellery and cash. ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/lucknow/unhappily-ever-after-daku-dulhanwho-duped-12-grooms-arrested-in-up/amp_articleshow/120803107.cms))

Police recovered Rs 72,000, a motorcycle, a gold mangalsutra, eleven mobile phones and three fake Aadhaar cards, according to the report. A borrower says a sale agreement for ₹2 lakh was actually security for a ₹1.5 lakh loan carrying roughly 36% annual interest, with property papers taken as additional security and repayment spread over thirty-six instalments.

items.title: The Sheo Grid Ghost Shift
items.one_line: Night workers at a Rajasthan power station hear trucks, see stones thrown and report a dead worker’s ghost—while police suspect someone is clearing the station for theft.
items.mechanism: A supposedly haunted electricity sub-station becomes an overnight battleground where employees, tantriks and police interpret unexplained sounds and movement as either ghosts or a cover for equipment theft.
items.engine: Every night shift creates a live locked-location mystery: protect the station, identify the intruder, test the haunting and decide whether the dead worker is warning them or hiding the crime.

cast.motive: Survive night duty and force authorities to take the haunting seriously.
The workers connect the supernatural activity to his death on duty.
Prove the presence is spiritual while avoiding responsibility for failing to remove it.
Keep the grid operating and prevent panic among staff.
Find a practical explanation and stop a possible equipment theft.
Use fear and darkness to move government equipment—or remain falsely accused.

reasons: The incident is recent enough that workers and officials may be identifiable.
Change the station, district, employee details and the reported death.
Use a fictional utility site and keep the ghost-versus-theft question unresolved.

prior_adaptations: The general haunted-workplace premise is common, but no specific adaptation of the Sheo grid sub-station incident was identified in the sources opened.
items.why_this_sells: Indian listeners understand the terror of being ordered to work alone at night in a remote government facility where even the police cannot explain what is happening.
items.why_not: The raw incident may be a short theft scare rather than a true haunting, so the serial needs a fictional hidden network behind the nightly disturbances.

items.title: The Factory That Lost Its Money to Ghosts
items.one_line: A failing family factory is declared haunted by a tantrik, who performs rituals, promises money will materialise and warns that a daughter will die if the spirit is not removed.
items.mechanism: A spiritual fraudster converts business losses into a supernatural diagnosis, repeatedly stages rituals inside the factory and uses the alleged ghost to extract money and obedience.
items.engine: The factory’s debt, failed rituals and escalating supernatural threats keep the family returning to the healer, while each new ritual can expose another accomplice or deepen the possibility of a staged haunting.

cast.motive: Save a heavily indebted business and believe the supernatural explanation for its losses.
Recover the factory and money while deciding whether to expose the spiritualist.
Use fear of ghosts and promises of magical wealth to extract repeated payments.

cast.name_or_role: The tantrik’s uncle and ritual accomplices
cast.motive: Perform staged voices, bundles and money rituals while remaining hidden behind the spiritual authority.
Keep working despite the haunting claims and unexplained nighttime activity.
Recover the industrial loan as the owners chase occult solutions.

reasons: The court record concerns identifiable complainants and accused persons.
Change the factory, city, amounts, family relationships and spiritualist identity.
Frame the supernatural elements as allegations and staged claims, not established fact.

prior_adaptations: The broad idea of a fraudster using exorcism to exploit a family is familiar, but the specific factory, staged money bundles and threatened daughter were not found as a named film or series adaptation.
items.why_this_sells: The fear is brutally immediate: when a business collapses, someone tells the family the building is haunted—and charges them to save it.
items.why_not: The case ultimately reads more clearly as occult fraud than supernatural intrusion, so its horror depends on atmosphere and the possibility that one unexplained event was real.

items.title: The Haunted House Instagram Trap
items.one_line: A young online tantrik sends a woman fake ghost images, convinces her that spirits occupy her home and turns a private fear into a nationwide ritual business.
items.mechanism: An occultist uses Instagram advertising, fabricated ghost images and remote rituals to make victims believe their homes are haunted, then demands payment for exorcism.
items.engine: Every new follower can become a victim, every alleged spirit can require another paid ritual and every police tracing step can reveal a larger digital network.

cast.motive: Remove the supposed spirits and recover money after the healer stops responding.
Scale fear through social media while hiding behind aliases and paid advertising.
Solve family and personal problems through increasingly expensive rituals.
Trace accounts, phone numbers, bank transactions and the operator’s real identity.
Profit from or conceal the digital pipeline that feeds victims to the healer.

reasons: The incident is recent and involves living private individuals.
Change all names, online handles, locations and victim details.
Build the serial around a fictional composite of multiple complaints rather than exposing one real complainant.

prior_adaptations: Online occult scams are a familiar news pattern, but no specific dramatisation of this 2025 Delhi–Rajasthan case was identified in the sources opened.
items.why_this_sells: The listener’s own home and phone become the haunted location when a stranger can send a fake ghost image and make the fear feel real.
items.why_not: Its real mechanism is sustained fraud rather than an unexplained supernatural presence, placing it close to THE LONG DECEPTION.

items.title: The Man With Two Wives, Two Names and Two Vehicle Registrations
items.one_line: In Odisha, one travelling-business owner allegedly lived as Bitu Biswas in Jajpur and Soleman Shaik in Murshidabad, with a wife, identity documents and vehicle attached to each life. ([newindianexpress.com](https://www.newindianexpress.com/states/odisha/2019/Dec/22/man-with-two-aadhaar-and-two-voter-ids-found-in-odishas-jajpur-2079545.html))
items.where: Jajpur Road, Odisha and Murshidabad, West Bengal, India
items.mechanism: Two parallel identities were allegedly maintained across state lines: separate Aadhaar and voter IDs, separate marriages, separate vehicles and separate local histories. ([newindianexpress.com](https://www.newindianexpress.com/states/odisha/2019/Dec/22/man-with-two-aadhaar-and-two-voter-ids-found-in-odishas-jajpur-2079545.html))
items.engine: Each family, document, business contact and government record can discover a contradiction that threatens to collapse the other household.

cast.motive: Maintaining two marriages, businesses and social worlds without letting either family meet
Protecting her marriage and discovering what the husband’s documents conceal
Believing the second identity is the man’s only real life
Following a businessman whose records and promises do not match
Linking two names, two states and two sets of identity documents

reasons: The report concerns a living private individual and an FIR-stage investigation.
Change names, religion, districts, businesses, documents and the precise family structure.
Treat the identity allegations as allegations unless a court record establishes them.

items.why_this_sells: It turns the everyday Indian document trail—Aadhaar, voter ID, vehicle papers and marriage records—into a ticking bomb between two ordinary households.
items.why_not: The available report is only a short FIR-based account, so its engine is powerful but the emotional and investigative middle is largely undocumented.

items.title: The Railway Officer Who Had Seventy-Two Wives
items.one_line: A Bihar man allegedly posed as a railway employee, married women across Bihar and West Bengal, lived in each house just long enough to earn trust, then disappeared after a fake transfer. ([newindianexpress.com](https://www.newindianexpress.com/nation/2014/Jun/04/married-72-times-tte-gets-jail-ticket-621013.html))
items.mechanism: Mohammad Sijam allegedly used more than a dozen aliases, changed religious presentation according to the bride’s family, wore a TTE uniform and treated each marriage as a temporary station posting. ([newindianexpress.com](https://www.newindianexpress.com/nation/2014/Jun/04/married-72-times-tte-gets-jail-ticket-621013.html))
items.engine: Every new village is a fresh recruitment market, and every marriage produces a new household, alias, transfer story and delayed discovery.

cast.motive: Cash, jewellery, status and the ability to reinvent himself at every station

cast.name_or_role: The first wife to suspect the pattern
cast.motive: Finding the missing husband and proving that the disappearance is not an ordinary transfer
Believing she has married a government employee with a secure future
Comparing clues and discovering they are all married to the same man
Tracing a fake employee across districts and aliases

reasons: The case is recent enough that private individuals and alleged victims may still be identifiable.
Change the accused’s name, railway zone, districts, religious presentation and all bride details.
Avoid presenting the reported number of marriages as a judicially verified count unless court records are located.

items.why_this_sells: The listener understands the promise immediately: a railway job means stability, and the horror is discovering that the government uniform was the disguise.
items.why_not: The mechanism is exceptionally long-running, but the article gives little detail about the first marriages, the supporting network or how the wives’ lives changed after the arrest.

items.title: The Family That Became a Different Family in Every City
items.one_line: A Delhi family allegedly rotated through fake relatives, Navy-officer identities, army-doctor credentials and multiple marriages while using forged demand drafts to move through jewellers, car dealerships and wealthy households. ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/delhi/fantastic-4-used-fake-dds-to-buy-luxuries-duped-many/articleshow/64239884.cms))
items.where: Delhi, Punjab, Chandigarh, Goa and Mumbai, India
items.mechanism: The Kaul family allegedly performed different kinship arrangements and professional identities: relatives of a Navy officer, a retired army doctor, a fake couple and multiple marital histories, all supporting a travelling fraud operation. ([timesofindia.indiatimes.com](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/delhi/fantastic-4-used-fake-dds-to-buy-luxuries-duped-many/articleshow/64239884.cms))
items.engine: The family’s survival depends on continuously changing who each member is to the next target while preserving a believable shared history.

cast.motive: Access to money, jewellery and socially respectable victims

cast.name_or_role: The father posing as a retired army doctor
cast.motive: Legitimacy, access to institutions and control of the family operation

cast.name_or_role: The mother and sister posing as relatives
cast.motive: Creating emotional credibility and reducing suspicion at the point of sale
Trusting a marriage proposal that is actually an extraction scheme
Recovering goods purchased with forged instruments after the family disappears

reasons: The case involves living or recently living private individuals and police allegations.
Change names, family composition, cities, professions, victims and the exact financial instruments.
Use the family’s shifting performances as fiction rather than asserting every reported offence as proven.

items.why_this_sells: The fear is domestic and recognisable: the people introduced as your relatives, in-laws or respectable professionals may all be actors in one travelling family business.
items.why_not: Its many fraud methods compete for attention, so the adaptation must choose the family’s rotating identities as the spine instead of becoming a generic scam anthology.
